To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

influenza virus has antioncogenic (AOA) activity against polyoma virus induced sarcomas in rats, that the AOA is due to influenza virus, that it depends on the relative doses used, that the AOTA is reduced by storage of the vaccine, and that the mechanism of AOA is at least partially due interference with polyoma virus multiplication.

the antioncogeneic effect of influenza virus on polyomavirus-induced tumors in newborn Wistrats can be attributed, in part, to the interference of influenza virus on adsorption of polyomavirus on rat embryo fiboblast cells.

influenza virus reduces significantly the oncogenicity of polyoma virus by interfering with polyoma virus multiplication in vivo, and by inhibiting the adsorption of the latter virus on target cells in vitro.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and testing of an experimental model for the investigation of antioncogenic agents in the rat.
the possible use of influenza virus as a vaccine against cancer.
the antioncogenetic activity of the A/PR 8/34 (Hon1) strain of the influenza virus in newborn Wister rats inoculated simultaneously with polyoma virus.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the AOA of influenza A/PR8 virus is due to interference of the virus with polyoma multiplication in vivo and to interference with polyoma virus multiplication on rat embryo fibrotast cells in vitro.
AOA was probably due to interference of A/PR 8/34 (HO N1) influenza virus with polyomavirus adsorption on target rat cells.
AOA was probably due to the interference of influenza virus on the multiplication and/or adsorption of polyomavirus in target cells.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the oncogenic activity of influenza virus is due at least in part to the interference of influenza virus infection with the adsorption of oncogenic polyoma virus on target cells.
influenza virus has an AOA on polyoma virus-induced tumors in newborn Wister rats.
influenza virus is able to interfere significantly with polyoma virus induced oncogenesis in newborn Wistar rat.
The main takeaway from our work is that
influenza virus has antioncogenic properties in vivo, and this property may be due to interference with the adsorption of the polyoma virus to its target cell.
influenza virus can reduce the adsorption of other viruses on target cells, thus interfering with their oncogenic activity.
the antioncogene activity of influenza virus is due to the virus itself and not to any other material possibly present in the virus suspension.
